newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Germany's Kohl pledges EU will crack down on crime.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Kohl pledges EU will crack down on crime.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl promised the European Union's 300 million citizens on Wednesday that the bloc would crack down on drugs and crime.

"I do believe that the citizens of Europe expect us to show great determination in combating crime and ... particularly organised crime, the mafia and the drugs mafia in particular," Kohl told reporters on the first day of a visit to Ireland.

Kohl's words struck home in a country suffering what police say is a major drugs crisis and a crime wave. Its foremost investigative reporter, Veronica Guerin, was shot dead by killers believed hired by a drug baron earlier this year.
Kohl was speaking after talks with Irish Prime Minister John Bruton, whose country holds the current EU presidency and which will host the first of two summits in Dublin this weekend.

Kohl said Saturday's informal meeting would allow leaders to have a frank exchange on the progress of an inter-governmental conference (IGC) charged with recasting the bloc's founding treaties to streamline it for the 21st century.
"No decisions will be made. It's a brainstorming meeting... a stock-taking meeting to see what we have achieved already," Kohl told a news conference.
Among the issues to be discussed are foreign and security policy, the fight against crime and drug trafficking, and developments in central and eastern Europe, he said.
Earlier Kohl told the Irish parliament that the enlargement of the EU to include former Soviet bloc states was "not only a historic but a moral obligation."
"It is also in all our interests, political, economic and cultural. Warsaw, Budapest and Prague are just as much an integral part of Europe as Berlin, Paris and Dublin," he said.
"Especially for us Germans, it is inconceivable that Poland's Western frontier should ultimately remain the European Union's eastern border," said Kohl.
He also told Irish legislators that a single currency was necessary in order to secure Europe's economic future.

"In this we shall only succeed if monetary union is at the same time a union for stability. That is why the stability criteria cannot be tampered with. The same goes for the timetable; it makes for a healthy pressure."
He said if the timetable or the criteria for entry to EMU were postponed or changed for whatever reason, then people would find an excuse to change them again and again.

"There are certain things which have to happen and have to happen now and Germany will have to make a huge effort to reach the goal. The window of opportunity is not always there, it is not always open," he told reporters.

Asked if he thought Ireland would qualify for the first phase of EMU, Kohl said, "The criteria exist and Ireland will have to live up to the criteria like Germany. And I can tell you it's very difficult."
Kohl arrived in Dublin on Wednesday for the first official bilateral visit by a German chancellor since 1979. He last visited Ireland in 1990 to attend an EU Dublin summit.
Thursday is the anniversary of Germany's reunification in 1990 and Kohl was to host a Unity Day reception in the Irish capital before leaving for home.
